extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, authors, and meta-researchers interested in editorial/peer-review quality
extracted.subtask_description: Quantifying and analyzing errors that escape peer review and editorial processes in high-profile journals by defining indices, classifying mistakes by severity and location, measuring time-to-correction, and testing temporal trends and correlates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake Index Total (MIT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mistake Index Total (MIT) is the result of the division of the corrections published by the total number of items published in a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed as a percentage to facilitate comparison. MIT uses the total items (articles and other material indexed in WoS) published in a year, removing the Corrections. Useful for temporal trend analysis and cross-journal comparisons (e.g., MIT = 2.2 for Nature and PLOS ONE in 2014 despite differences in journal size and impact factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake Index Paper (MIP)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mistake Index Paper (MIP) is the result of the division of the corrections published by the total number of papers (articles category) published in a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed in percentage. In MIP no factor correction is applied (but elsewhere a correction factor may be applied to adjust for non-article corrections). MIP highlights errors relative to published papers specifically and is used alongside MIT to assess editorial quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction factor for WoS 'Corrections' category
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the 'Correction' category in WoS includes all items published with mistakes, not only articles, a correction factor is applied taking into account the average proportion of corrections affecting papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example factors used in the study: 70.15% for Nature, 39.54% for Science, 97.72% for PNAS. Apply this factor to total corrections when estimating paper-specific mistake rates from WoS 'Corrections' counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake severity classification (mild / moderate / severe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mild: typographical or minor grammatical error (typos, mistakes in the title, address, email address, footnote, author name, or acknowledgements). Moderate: affected the paper to some degree but not substantially, impacting sentences, figures, results, or references (mistakes in values, equations, figure axes, table and figure legends). Severe: substantial mistakes such as important modifications in figures, results or conclusions, implying major changes (figure substantial modifications, re-interpretation of the results, clarification of the conclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a qualitative variable only considering mistakes that appeared in articles. Also note when corrections were due to editorial/printer error (e.g., after author galley proof). Severity categories were used to report proportions (47.7% moderate, 34.7% mild, 17.6% severe in the analyzed sample) and to analyze time-to-correction differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-to-correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Time-to-correction is defined as the interval in days between the publication of the original item and the date of publication of the correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess performance in the correction process. Severe mistakes take significantly longer to correct (study: severe 467.96 ± 602.46 d vs mild 185.89 ± 704.85 d and moderate 198.97 ± 320.17 d). Trend analyses of time-to-correction can reveal increasing delays and inform recommendations to publish corrections promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake location / category (figures, authors, references, results, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of where mistakes occur in the paper (e.g., figures, authors, references, results). In the study, 60% of mistakes were related to figures, authors, references or results; figures were involved in 32% of corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures accounted for a disproportionate share of moderate and severe mistakes (41.3% of severe mistakes, 49.3% of moderate mistakes); figures and results together account for 79.4% of severe mistakes. Guidance: reviewers, authors and editors should prioritize checking figures and results to reduce corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling rule for correction analysis (30 corrections/year)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each journal the study analyzed 30 corrections/year selected at random, totalling 1,980 mistakes (660 per journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 30 corrections/year was considered representative for statistical analyses because it represented on average ~47% of corrections published in Nature, ~34% in Science and ~28% in PNAS during the study period. Use random sampling and report representativeness relative to total corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of retractions and misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The analyses excluded corrections related to retractions and misconduct; the corrections analyzed are material outside of misconduct and retraction issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative analyses focused only on mistakes appearing in articles (n = 1,428). Explicitly exclude retractions/misconduct to focus on editorial/authorial errors amendable by correction rather than ethical breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods and trend-detection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal trends assessed with Spearman rank coefficient; inter-group differences tested using ANOVA and Chi-square; Cusum test applied to detect temporal changes in index trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cusum details provided: St = sum_{i=1}^t (x̄_t - μ); for positive displacement plot St = sum (x̄_t - μ - k) where k is half the displacement to be detected; decision interval = 5k; k and decision interval chosen using average run length (ARL); significance level α = 0.002. Use these methods to detect small but cumulative changes in mistake indices over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation testing of mistake indices with journal metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Test for relationship between MIT/MIP and journal impact factor or number of items published (Spearman correlation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found no relationship (e.g., rs = 0.123, p = 0.651 between MIT and impact factor). Use these analyses to evaluate whether editorial quality (as measured) correlates with conventional journal metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of responsibility (editorial/printing vs author)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record whether corrections arose from printing/editorial errors (e.g., mistake introduced in printing after author galley correction) versus author-origin errors (e.g., misspelling, missing co-author, incorrect address).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report percentages by journal (printing process responsible for 5% of mistakes in Nature, 2.7% in Science, 18.4% in PNAS). Note that ~13% of mistakes were author-category, indicating superficial review by authors/editors. Use attribution to guide where process improvements are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of correction frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Two possible interpretations of an increasing number of published corrections: (1) decreasing quality of peer-review and editorial processes, or (2) increased detection and willingness to publish corrections (which may itself indicate editorial quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal pattern is important; low number of corrections might indicate unwillingness to acknowledge errors. Use contextual interpretation rather than assuming more corrections always mean poorer quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritization guidance for reviewers/editors/authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide guidelines that focus reviewers, authors and editors on areas most associated with mistakes (especially figures and results) and on reducing time-to-correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because figures are implicated heavily in severe and moderate mistakes, make figure checks a priority during peer review and editorial checks. Encourage prompt publication of corrections, and consider process changes to reduce delays in correcting severe mistakes (which averaged ~1.23 years to publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and incentive recommendations for improving review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations include seeking effective incentives for reviewers (e.g., a recognized reviewer quality index) and promoting post-publication peer review as part of the editorial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reviewers work without extrinsic rewards and time constraints are a handicap (reviewers spend on average 2–6 hours reviewing a paper), journals should explore incentives (citations: Hauser & Fehr 2007; Paoletti 2009) and facilitate post-publication reader peer review to improve overall quality and error detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on detecting moderate mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Although severe mistakes are impactful, moderate mistakes constituted the largest share (47.7% in study) and should be a focus for detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate mistakes (mistakes in values, equations, figure axes, table/figure legends) can affect interpretation; focusing on their detection during peer review/editorial checks can reduce the overall correction burden and prevent propagation of errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of temporal segmentation (Cusum) to detect shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Cusum analysis to index time series to identify points where index trends shift significantly (e.g., study detected shifts in MIT around 2008 for Nature and different periods for Science and PNAS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cusum plots with warning lines and decision intervals can signal significant increases in mistake indices; use to monitor when editorial practices or detection rates change over time and to trigger process reviews.
